questions.prompt: State what it means for a rule \(f:A\to B\) to be a function.
questions.answer: A rule \(f:A\to B\) is a function if every input in the domain \(A\) is assigned exactly one output in the codomain \(B\). One input cannot have two different outputs.

questions.prompt: If \(f:A\to B\), name the set \(A\).
questions.answer: The set \(A\) is the domain. It is the set of permitted inputs for the function.

Set the function equal to \(13\):
\[
2x+5=13
\]
Subtract \(5\):
\[
2x=8
\]
Divide by \(2\):
\[
x=4
\]

questions.prompt: Find the natural real domain of \(f(x)=\frac{1}{x-2}\).
questions.answer:
The denominator cannot be zero. Require
\[
x-2\ne0
\]
so
\[
x\ne2
\]
The natural real domain is all real numbers except \(2\).

questions.prompt: Given \(f(x)=x+1\) and \(g(x)=2x\), find \((g\circ f)(3)\).
Determine whether the rule assigning \(x\) to both \(x^2\) and \(-x^2\) is a function from \(\mathbb R\) to \(\mathbb R\).
questions.answer:
It is not a function because most inputs have two outputs. For example, when \(x=2\), the rule assigns both
\[
2^2=4
\]
and
\[
-2^2=-4
\]
A function must assign exactly one output to each input.

questions.prompt: Find \((f\circ g)(x)\) and \((g\circ f)(x)\) for \(f(x)=x+3\) and \(g(x)=x^2\).
questions.answer:
Compute \(f(g(x))\):
\[
(f\circ g)(x)=f(x^2)=x^2+3
\]
Compute \(g(f(x))\):
\[
(g\circ f)(x)=g(x+3)=(x+3)^2
\]
In general these are different.

questions.prompt: Show that \(f(x)=2x+1\) is one-to-one on \(\mathbb R\).
questions.answer:
Assume \(f(x_1)=f(x_2)\). Then
\[
2x_1+1=2x_2+1
\]
Subtract \(1\):
\[
2x_1=2x_2
\]
Divide by \(2\):
\[
x_1=x_2
\]
Therefore \(f\) is one-to-one.

questions.prompt: Explain why \(f(x)=x^2\) is not one-to-one on \(\mathbb R\).
questions.answer:
A function is one-to-one if different inputs never produce the same output. But
\[
f(2)=2^2=4
\]
and
\[
f(-2)=(-2)^2=4
\]
Since \(2\ne-2\) but the outputs are equal, \(f(x)=x^2\) is not one-to-one on \(\mathbb R\).

questions.prompt: A position model is \(s(t)=5t^2\) for \(t\ge0\). What is the domain, and what does \(s(3)\) mean?
questions.answer:
The domain is \(t\ge0\), because time in this model is non-negative. Evaluate
\[
s(3)=5(3)^2=45
\]
This means the model assigns position \(45\) at time \(t=3\), in whatever position units the model uses.

questions.prompt: Determine the range of \(f(x)=x^2+1\) for real \(x\).
questions.answer:
For all real \(x\),
\[
x^2\ge0
\]
Therefore
\[
x^2+1\ge1
\]
The smallest value occurs at \(x=0\), giving \(f(0)=1\). The range is
\[
[1,\infty)
\]

questions.prompt: For \(f(x)=\sqrt{x-4}\), find the natural real domain and explain the restriction.
questions.answer:
The expression under the square root must be non-negative:
\[
x-4\ge0
\]
So
\[
x\ge4
\]
The natural real domain is \([4,\infty)\). Values less than \(4\) would make the square root of a negative number in the real-number setting.

questions.prompt: For \(f(x)=\frac{x+1}{x-3}\), find the natural domain and solve \(f(x)=2\).
questions.answer:
The denominator cannot be zero, so \(x\ne3\). Solve
\[
\frac{x+1}{x-3}=2
\]
Multiply by \(x-3\), with \(x\ne3\):
\[
x+1=2x-6
\]
So
\[
7=x
\]
The solution is \(x=7\), which is allowed because \(7\ne3\).

questions.prompt: Determine whether \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\), \(f(x)=x^3\), is onto.
questions.answer:
To be onto \(\mathbb R\), every real \(y\) must equal \(x^3\) for some real \(x\). Given any real \(y\), choose
\[
x=\sqrt[3]{y}
\]
Then
\[
f(x)=(\sqrt[3]{y})^3=y
\]
So \(f\) is onto \(\mathbb R\).

questions.prompt: Determine whether \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\), \(f(x)=x^2\), is onto.
questions.answer:
It is not onto \(\mathbb R\). The outputs of \(x^2\) are always non-negative:
\[
x^2\ge0
\]
For example, there is no real \(x\) such that \(x^2=-1\). Since \(-1\) is in the codomain \(\mathbb R\) but is not an output, the function is not onto.

questions.prompt: Diagnose the error: because \((f\circ g)(x)=(g\circ f)(x)\) for one value of \(x\), the two compositions are the same function.
questions.answer:
Two functions are equal only if they give the same output for every input in their common domain. Agreement at one input is not enough. For example, with \(f(x)=x+1\) and \(g(x)=x^2\),
\[
(f\circ g)(x)=x^2+1
\]
while
\[
(g\circ f)(x)=(x+1)^2
\]
They may agree at some values but are not the same function.

questions.prompt: Prove that the composition of two one-to-one functions is one-to-one.
questions.answer:
Let \(f:A\to B\) and \(g:B\to C\) be one-to-one. Suppose
\[
(g\circ f)(x_1)=(g\circ f)(x_2)
\]
Then
\[
g(f(x_1))=g(f(x_2))
\]
Since \(g\) is one-to-one,
\[
f(x_1)=f(x_2)
\]
Since \(f\) is one-to-one,
\[
x_1=x_2
\]
Therefore \(g\circ f\) is one-to-one.

questions.prompt: Give an example of a function that is one-to-one but not onto \(\mathbb R\), and justify both claims.
questions.answer:
Let \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be \(f(x)=e^x\). It is one-to-one because if
\[
e^{x_1}=e^{x_2}
\]
then \(x_1=x_2\). It is not onto \(\mathbb R\) because \(e^x>0\) for every real \(x\), so no input gives an output such as \(-1\) or \(0\).
